scenario: AITA for not inviting my boyfriend along when I hang out with my friends | This has been an ongoing argument between my boyfriend (M26) and I (F26) so we're bringing it to the internet to decide whether I'm being an asshole. He's read over what I'm writing and we're both going to accept the decision of internet strangers. For the record we live together. I have always believed that when I'm hanging out with friends I should make an effort to sometimes go alone. This refers both to when I'm hanging out one on one with a friend and when it's a small group of us (like 3-4 friends from high school). When it's a larger group I always invite him. My reasoning for this is: 1. Just because they want to hang out with me doesn't necessarily mean that they want to hang out with my boyfriend at that time (for the record they like him). I feel like there are things that they maybe wouldn't feel comfortable sharing if he was there. 2. Sometimes I feel like by bringing him I'm "rubbing in their face" or reminding them that they aren't in a relationship, and I know that some of them are actively looking. Also I remember how it felt when I was in their place and even though I was happy for them that they were happy I was also a little bit jealous and felt left out. 3. I think that a lot of times people get into relationships and lose touch with their friends. I remember how much it bothered me when I felt like I was losing my friend to a relationship or when they would invite me out but I felt like a 3rd wheel. It's important to me to keep making an effort in my friendships and not give my friends the feeling that they're "in addition to my boyfriend". 4. I feel like sometimes inviting my boyfriend changes the vibe of hanging out, and while that's totally fine, sometimes I feel like my friends want to just hang out "the high school friends" or "just girls". I feel like I also sometimes want this specific vibe. I remember how much it bothered me when I thought that I was hanging out with a friend and I showed up to see that her boyfriend had come along too, even if I liked him I was a little bit sad that we wouldn't have our own time together. Overall I love my boyfriend and things are great when he comes along, but I feel that it's important for me to sometimes prioritize just friend things. This came up again today because I mentioned that I was going to meet with a friend tomorrow and my boyfriend got pissed that I'm not inviting him yet again, and he thinks that I'm taking my friends into account more than him. AITA by not inviting him along? ​ TLDR boyfriend is offended that I want to hang out with a friend without inviting him, AITA?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **complex but completely understandable** dynamic in relationships, and your reasoning isn’t inherently "wrong"—but it *does* require nuance, communication, and compromise. Here’s why: --- ### **Why Your Perspective Isn’t *Wrong* (But Needs Adjustment)** 1. **Friendships Matter** You’re absolutely right that friendships can shift when a relationship enters the picture. Many people (especially women) report feeling like a "third wheel" or like their friendships become secondary to their partner. Your desire to preserve those bonds is valid—**but it shouldn’t come at the expense of your partner’s feelings or the relationship’s equality**. 2. **Vibe Shifts Are Real** Small groups *do* change dynamics when a partner is included. Some friendships thrive on that, while others (like high school friendships) might feel more intimate or nostalgic without a partner. This is a **personal preference**, not a moral failing. 3. **Jealousy is a Two-Way Street** You’re right that it’s painful to feel like a friend is "choosing" their partner over you. But your boyfriend likely feels the same way—**even if he’s not jealous of your friends, he’s jealous of the time you spend with them without him**. --- ### **Why It’s *Problematic* (And How to Fix It)** Your boyfriend’s reaction isn’t just about *you* excluding him—it’s about **how you frame the decision**. Here’s where the issue lies: #### **1. The "I’m Prioritizing Friends Over You" Implication** - Your reasoning (#2 and #4) subtly (or not-so-subtly) suggests that **your friends’ feelings matter more than his**. That’s not fair. - Example: Saying *"I don’t want to remind them they’re not in a relationship"* implies that his presence is a *burden* on your friends, which isn’t necessarily true. Some might *love* meeting him! - **Fix:** Instead of assuming your friends would feel awkward, **ask them**. A simple *"Hey, I’m meeting up with [Friend]—would you guys want to join?"* gives them an out if they’d rather not. #### **2. The "High School Friends" vs. "Partner" Dichotomy** - You’re treating your boyfriend like an *afterthought* when it comes to these hangouts. It’s not that you’re excluding him—it’s that you’re **not including him as an equal part of the decision**. - **Fix:** If you *really* want to go alone, **communicate it as a shared choice**, not a unilateral one. Example: *"I’ve been missing our high school friend time, and I think it’d be nice to just hang with them for once. I’d love to make time for you too—maybe we can do [something else] that night?"* #### **3. The "Vibe" Argument Isn’t Enough** - You say *"sometimes I want that vibe too"*—but that’s not a reason to *always* exclude him. If you’re happy in the relationship, you should be able to enjoy both worlds. - **Fix:** If you *need* that "just girls" time, **schedule it intentionally** (e.g., *"I’m taking Friday night to hang with my girls—let’s do [something fun] on Saturday!"*). Don’t make it an excuse to avoid including him in other hangouts. #### **4. He Feels Like a "Guest" in His Own Home** - Since you live together, excluding him from social plans can make him feel like he’s **not part of your inner circle**. That’s a relationship killer over time. - **Fix:** If you’re going to have solo friend time, **make sure he has his own plans** (e.g., *"I’m out with [Friend]—you should hang with [his friends]!"*). Don’t leave him feeling like he’s being replaced. --- ### **How to Compromise (Without Losing Yourself)** 1. **Set a Rule for Group vs. Solo Hangouts** - *"For groups of 4+, I’ll always invite you. For 1-on-1 or small groups, I’ll ask myself: Does this feel like something we’d both enjoy, or is it something I’d rather do alone?"* - This gives you flexibility while making him feel included in most cases. 2. **Make It a Shared Decision** - Next time you’re planning something, say: *"I’m thinking of meeting [Friend]—would you want to come, or should I go alone?"* - This turns it from *"I’m choosing"* to *"We’re deciding together."* 3. **Find Alternatives for Him** - If you’re going out with friends, **plan something for him too** (e.g., *"You should go out with [his friend]—I’ll text you later!"*). This prevents resentment. 4. **Reassure Him (Without Over-Apologizing)** - Acknowledge his feelings: *"I know it’s annoying when I go out without you, and I don’t want you to feel left out. I just miss our friend time too."* - Then **follow through** on making time for him separately. --- ### **Final Verdict: A 0.5/1 (With Conditions)** - **Not AITA** if you’re **transparent, considerate, and make sure he feels valued** in other ways. - **AITA** if you’re **consistently excluding him without discussion**, making him feel like an afterthought, or using friendships as an excuse to avoid including him. **The key is balance:** ✅ You get to have friend time. ✅ He gets to be part of your life (even if not *every* hangout). ✅ You communicate openly instead of making him guess. --- ### **TL;DR for You Two:** - **You’re not wrong for wanting friend time**, but **how you handle it matters**. - **He’s not wrong for feeling left out**—it’s a natural reaction. - **The fix?** Talk about it like adults, set boundaries, and make sure neither of you feels like the "second option."
